title: Church Bells Ringing, Rainy Winter Night
medium: Watercolor and gouache over graphite on wove paper

image.credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Mrs. Louise M. Dunn in memory of Henry G. Keller (1949.544)
image.license: Public domain. Released under the Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access program

altText: A watercolor of a church spire rising between two houses on a rainy winter night.

source.verifiedBy: Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access API record (title, creators, creation_date, technique, culture, creditline, description, did_you_know, images.web.url, share_license_status CC0)

context: A watercolor and gouache work by Charles Burchfield, made in December 1917. The Cleveland Museum of Art says Burchfield regarded it as one of his best works from his 'golden year'. It shows a church spire rising between two houses and reflects his childhood fear of the church bell.

descriptions.k: Look at the tall church spire between two houses. It is a rainy winter night. Church bells are ringing. What do you think the bells sound like? Point to the spire.
descriptions.g12: Charles Burchfield painted a church spire between two houses on a rainy winter night. The bells are ringing. He painted this when he was a young artist. Look at the whole picture. What do you think the ringing sounds like? Does it make you feel calm or nervous?
descriptions.g35: Charles Burchfield made this watercolor in December 1917, during what he called his golden year. A church spire rises between two houses on a rainy winter night as the bells ring. He remembered being afraid of the church bell as a child. Look at how he paints a sound you cannot see. What details help you hear the bells?
descriptions.g68: Burchfield made this watercolor and gouache in December 1917 and regarded it as one of his best works from his golden year. A spire rises between two houses on a rainy winter night, and the picture reflects his childhood fear of the church bell. The museum notes he calmed himself by thinking about Christmas. How does he turn sound and feeling into things you can see?
descriptions.g910: Burchfield's December 1917 watercolor and gouache shows a church spire between two houses on a rainy winter night and reflects his childhood fear of the bell. He calmed himself then by thinking of Christmas, and he considered this among his best works of that year. The church in Salem has since been destroyed by fire. How does the picture make an invisible sound a visual and emotional experience?
descriptions.g1112: In this December 1917 watercolor and gouache, Burchfield transforms a church spire between two houses on a rainy winter night into an image of sound and memory. The museum links it to his childhood fear of the church bell, which he soothed by thinking of Christmas, and notes that he counted it among his finest works of his golden year. How do the picture's choices turn private memory into shared experience, and what do we lose knowing the church was later destroyed?

k.daily: Find the church spire. Where is it in the picture?
k.emotion: The bells are ringing at night. Does it feel cozy or a little scary to you?
k.observation: Point to the two houses. What is between them?
k.analysis: What do you think the bells sound like? Say it out loud.
k.line: Trace the tall spire with your finger. Which way does it point?
k.shape: The houses and the spire are made of shapes. Which shapes can you find?
k.color: It is a dark, rainy night. Which colors do you see?
k.texture: Imagine rain falling on the houses. How would it feel on your hand?
k.space: Find the spire and the houses. Which one is the tallest?
k.light: Where do you see light in the dark night?
k.meaning: Why do you think the bells are ringing on a rainy night?
k.culture: Long ago, church bells rang in towns. When have you heard a bell ring?
k.technique: This painting is made with watercolor, which is paint mixed with water. Where do you see the water in it?
k.personal: What would you do on a rainy winter night like this?
k.critical: How would you feel if you heard these bells outside your window?

g12.daily: Why do you think the painter chose a rainy night for a picture of ringing bells?
g12.emotion: What feeling does the dark night give you: calm, spooky or both?
g12.observation: List five things you can find in the picture, starting with the spire.
g12.analysis: Why does your eye go to the spire before the houses?
g12.line: How do the lines of the tall spire and the roofs lead your eyes up and down?
g12.shape: Which shapes do you see in the houses and the church, and how are they different?
g12.color: How do the dark colors and the lighter spots work together on a rainy night?
g12.texture: How did the painter use watery paint to show a rainy night?
g12.space: How does the spire between two houses help you feel it is tall and close?
g12.light: Where is the lightest part of the picture, and what makes it stand out?
g12.meaning: The painter was a little afraid of the church bell when he was a child. Where do you see that feeling in the picture?
g12.culture: This is a town in America over a hundred years ago. What does the picture tell you about the town?
g12.technique: Watercolor is paint mixed with water. How might that help show rain?
g12.personal: Tell about a sound you remember from when you were small, good or scary.
g12.critical: How would the picture feel different if it were a sunny day?

g35.daily: Which details show that this is a rainy winter night, and how do they affect the mood?
g35.emotion: What mood does the dark scene and tall spire create, and what shows you?
g35.observation: Describe the houses on either side of the spire. How are they placed?
g35.analysis: How does the spire between the two houses organize the picture?
g35.line: How do upright lines of the spire and rooflines guide your eye across the scene?
g35.shape: How do the shapes of the houses compare with the shape of the church spire?
g35.color: How do the colors of the night sky compare with the colors used for the buildings?
g35.texture: The artist used watercolor and gouache, an opaque water-based paint. How might each help show a wet, dim night?
g35.space: How does the spire rising between two houses make you feel small or close to it?
g35.light: Where do you find light in this dark scene, and how does it change the mood?
g35.meaning: The museum says Burchfield was afraid of the church bell as a child. How might this picture show a sound you can feel?
g35.culture: What does the picture suggest about life in a small American town in 1917?
g35.technique: Why might Burchfield have used watercolor for a night scene with rain?
g35.personal: What sound do you find hard to describe, and how would you paint it?
g35.critical: How can you tell whether the painter wants you to feel scared, comforted or both?

g68.daily: How does Burchfield use the vertical spire between two houses to give structure to a scene about sound?
g68.emotion: How do the dark tones of a rainy night work with the subject of ringing bells to create tension?
g68.observation: Compare the way the spire is painted with the way the houses are painted. What differences do you notice?
g68.analysis: How does the arrangement of the spire and houses create a feeling of confinement or protection?
g68.line: How do the upright lines of the spire, houses and rain create rhythm in the picture?
g68.shape: How do the angular forms of roofs and spire compare with the softer shapes of the night sky or rain?
g68.color: How does the artist's limited use of light against dark increase the drama of the night?
g68.texture: How might the watercolor and gouache create the damp surface and dim air of a rainy night?
g68.space: How does the viewpoint place the viewer in relation to the spire and the neighboring houses?
g68.light: How does the contrast between light and dark carry feeling as well as describing the weather?
g68.meaning: The museum says the picture reflects Burchfield's childhood fear of the church bell and his calming thought of Christmas. How does it hold both feelings?
g68.culture: How does the painting show a small American town in 1917 as a place of both comfort and unease?
g68.technique: How does the work show how an artist can paint something that cannot be seen, like a sound?
g68.personal: What memory of a sound or place from your childhood could become a picture, and how would you paint it?
g68.critical: How might the later destruction of the Salem church by fire change how you see the picture now?

g910.daily: How does the vertical emphasis of the spire between two houses create a hierarchy between sacred and domestic space?
g910.emotion: What tone do the dark tonal range and the rainy atmosphere establish, and how does it complicate the idea of a comforting church?
g910.observation: Examine how the paint handling differs among the spire, houses and surrounding space. What do those differences suggest about the artist's priorities?
g910.analysis: How does the compositional framing of the spire by the houses shape the way sound might seem to travel?
g910.line: How do repeated vertical and diagonal linear forms generate a sense of vibration?
g910.shape: How do geometric architectural shapes interact with expressive handling of the atmosphere?
g910.color: How does the contrast between light and dark in a night scene serve emotional ends beyond description?
g910.texture: How do watercolor and gouache allow Burchfield to produce both transparent atmosphere and denser, opaque passages?
g910.space: How does the viewpoint make the viewer a witness within the neighborhood rather than a distant observer?
g910.light: How does the depiction of light in darkness shape the psychological register of the scene?
g910.meaning: The museum links the picture to Burchfield's childhood fear of the church bell and his calming thought of Christmas. How does this context change how you read the spire?
g910.culture: How does a regional American scene of 1917 work as a vehicle for personal memory, and what does that reveal about the era's art?
g910.technique: How does the picture challenge the limits of visual art by trying to represent sound?
g910.personal: How do your own memories of sensory experience, such as bells, rain or storms, shape how you meet this picture?
g910.critical: What does it mean for a landmark in a picture to be destroyed later, and how does that affect the work's role as record?

g1112.daily: How does the vertical thrust of the spire, flanked by domestic structures, construct a tension between communal ritual and private domestic space?
g1112.emotion: In what ways might the tonal darkness of a rainy winter night transform the church bell from a comfort into a source of unease?
g1112.observation: Scan the junctions where architecture meets atmosphere. What do they reveal about Burchfield's attempt to make sound visible?
g1112.analysis: How does the compositional centering of the spire between two houses structure the viewer's sense of sound as radiating or pressing in?
g1112.line: How do linear patterns, from spire to rain, act as visual analogues of vibration and repetition?
g1112.shape: How does the interplay of rigid architectural forms and fluid watery passages produce an expressive rather than descriptive image?
g1112.color: How does the contrast of the night's light and dark operate as emotional rhetoric rather than a record of observation?
g1112.texture: How does the combination of watercolor and gouache suit the dual aims of atmosphere and structure in a work Burchfield considered among his best?
g1112.space: How does the implied vantage position the viewer inside the experience of a small-town night rather than outside it?
g1112.light: How might light in darkness be read here as both consolation and threat?
g1112.meaning: The museum ties the work to Burchfield's childhood fear of the church bell, which he calmed with thoughts of Christmas. How might this account support or complicate a reading of the work as expressionist?
g1112.culture: How does the picture mark the early flowering of a regional American modernism rooted in personal feeling?
g1112.technique: What are the challenges of translating sound into a still image, and what strategies does Burchfield appear to use?
g1112.personal: How does your own sense of memory and fear shape your response to a sacred object seen at night?
g1112.critical: How does the later loss of the Salem church to fire change the work's status as memory, and what responsibilities does that give a viewer?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Metadata-screened from the Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access API record (title, artist, date, medium, creditline, description, did_you_know, CC0 status). Church spire and houses on a rainy winter night; no nudity, violence or other sensitive content indicated in the record text. The record mentions the artist's childhood fear of the church bell; kept gentle in younger bands. The record gives the church as a Baptist church in Salem; I took Salem to be Salem, Ohio (Burchfield's hometown) from general knowledge, not from the record, so region should be confirmed. Movement label is the generally accepted one for Burchfield, not from the record. The image file has not been viewed; a person should confirm it before release.

teacherNote.context: A watercolor and gouache work over graphite on wove paper by Charles Burchfield, made in December 1917. The Cleveland Museum of Art says Burchfield regarded it as one of his best works from his golden year and that it shows a church spire rising between two houses and reflects his childhood fear of the church bell.
directions: Ask younger students to find the spire and the houses and describe what they think the bells sound like.
Have students paint a rainy night or a loud sound using watercolor, thinking about how to show something you hear.
Ask older students to discuss how an artist can use memory and feeling to paint something that is not visible, such as a sound.
